---
title: "Tracks and flight identity"
description: "How OPDI groups the position reports of one aircraft into tracks, divides a track that holds several flights, and gives each flight its identifier (flight_id), aircraft address, call sign and date of flight."
---

## In one sentence

A **track** is the run of position reports of one aircraft that belong
together; a track is one flight, or is divided into its flights when it
holds several, and each flight is one row of the flight list, identified by
`flight_id`.

## What it needs

- The **state vectors** of the OpenSky Network: one row per aircraft and
  second, built from the ADS-B messages (Automatic Dependent
  Surveillance–Broadcast) that aircraft send about once a second, with
  position, altitude, speed, heading and vertical rate.
- Two fields of each state vector identify the aircraft: the **ICAO 24-bit
  address** (`icao24`), six hexadecimal characters set in the transponder,
  which normally stays with one aircraft for years; and the **call sign**
  (`flt_id`), the radio name of the flight, which changes from flight to
  flight and is sometimes blank or garbled.

## How it is computed

1. **Thin.** When the state vectors are read, each aircraft's reports are
   thinned to one per 5 seconds: in each 5-second window the newest report is
   kept.
2. **Group by aircraft.** All reports with the same ICAO 24-bit address are
   taken together, in time order. The call sign is not part of the grouping,
   so a blank call sign does not start a track of its own.
3. **A new call sign starts a new track** only when it lasts: blank call
   signs are skipped, and a new call sign counts only if it stays the same for
   at least 30 s before the next change. It is compared with the last call
   sign heard in the previous 30 minutes. A call sign that flickers to a
   garbled value and back does not split the flight.
4. **A short silence at low altitude starts a new track.** If no report
   arrives for more than 15 minutes and the aircraft is below 5,000 ft when it
   is heard again, a new track starts: it may have landed and taken off again
   out of reception.
5. **A long silence starts a new track unless both sides fit one flight.** A
   silence of more than 30 minutes is a **gap**. The gap stays inside one
   track only when every check below passes; a check that lacks a value fails.

   | Check | Setting | Why |
   |---|---|---|
   | Gap not too long | at most 600 minutes | A longer silence leaves room for anything. |
   | En route before the gap | lowest of the 5 nearest altitudes within 5 minutes before the gap at or above 18,000 ft; if lower, climbing faster than 500 ft/min on at least 3 values | Lost at cruise or still climbing out. |
   | En route after the gap | the same at the other side; between 5,000 and 18,000 ft, descending faster than 500 ft/min on at least 3 values | Reappears in cruise or on its descent. |
   | No descent then climb | not both descending faster than 500 ft/min before and climbing faster than 500 ft/min after | That is what a stop inside the gap looks like. |
   | Call sign agrees | the last call sign before (at most 60 minutes old) and the first after (within 10 minutes) are not both present and different | A different call sign is a different flight. |
   | Straight-line speed | between 400 and 750 kt: the great-circle distance between the two sides divided by the time between them | A stop uses up time; faster than 750 kt means two aircraft share one address. |
   | Real address | not `000000`, `000001` or `ffffff` | These placeholder values are used by many aircraft. |

   The values at each side are read past blank reports, within 5 minutes of
   the gap, because position and altitude arrive in separate messages. A gap
   kept inside a track stays empty: no position is invented, and the event
   detectors work on each piece between gaps.
6. **Name the track.** The track identifier is the first 16 characters of
   the SHA-256 hash of the ICAO address, an underscore, and the time of the
   track's first report in seconds since 1970-01-01 (Unix time). A track with
   one flight keeps it as its `flight_id`.
7. **Date and call sign.** `dof` is the date of the track's first report: a
   track belongs to the day it starts, with all its reports even when it ends
   the next day. A day's run reads 11 hours of the previous day, so a gap near
   midnight is decided in the same way on both days. `flt_id` is the call sign
   the track broadcast most often, without the spaces OpenSky pads it with.

### The flights of a track {#flights-of-a-track}

8. **Several flights.** A track that contains a landing followed at least
   five minutes later by a take-off (`ALDT`, then `ATOT`) holds several
   flights, and the flight list has one row for each. A touch-and-go, a
   go-around and a rejected take-off do not divide a track.
9. **Where the track is divided.** At the in-block time (`AIBT`) after the
   landing; without one, at the midpoint between the landing and the
   take-off, or one second before the off-block time (`AOBT`) if that is
   earlier.
10. **Each flight** has its own airports, times, runways, stands and
    distance-circle crossings, and each event is published under the flight
    during which it happened.
11. **Names.** The flights of such a track are named `<track id>-L1`,
    `<track id>-L2` and so on, in time order. All of them have the `dof` of
    the track and are in the files of the day on which the track was first
    seen.

## Based on

- Developed for OPDI.
- The state vectors come from the [OpenSky Network](../resources.qmd#ref-schafer-2014); their
  fields and units are described in the [OpenSky API
  documentation](../resources.qmd#ref-opensky-api).
- Related published work: [Sun, Ellerbroek and Hoekstra (2017)](../resources.qmd#ref-sun-2017)
  cut ADS-B data into flights by clustering, a different method.

## What is published

Flight list columns `flight_id`, `icao24`, `flt_id` and `dof`. The same
`flight_id` is on every event of the flight in the flight events file.

## Use cases

- **Join the two files**: `flight_id` links each event to its flight-list row.
- **Join flights to tracks**: remove the ending `-L<number>` from `flight_id`.
- **Join with other data**: `icao24` with the date and the call sign, for
  example with aircraft registries or airline schedules (the call sign is
  often the airline code plus a flight number).
- **Daily traffic counts** per airport, with the movement columns (see
  [Counting movements](movements.qmd)).

## Limitations

A track can hold only part of a flight (reception lost), training circuits
with full stops at one airport stay one row, and placeholder addresses can
merge aircraft. See
[Limitations: tracks](../limitations.qmd#lim-tracks).
